title: Persistence and durability
summary: RDB snapshots with fork and copy-on-write, AOF logging with its three fsync policies, rewrite and the hybrid preamble format, and exactly what survives a restart under each configuration.

blocks.body:
Redis holds data in memory, but it offers two complementary persistence
mechanisms: **RDB** writes point-in-time binary snapshots, and **AOF** logs
every write command so the dataset can be replayed. You can run either, both,
or neither (a pure cache needs no persistence). The exam's core question: for a
given configuration, *how many seconds of writes can a crash lose?*

## RDB: point-in-time snapshots

RDB produces a compact binary file (`dump.rdb`) representing the dataset at one
moment. Snapshots happen on a schedule of **save points**:

```text
save 3600 1          # 1 change in 1 hour
save 300 100         # 100 changes in 5 minutes
save 60 10000        # 10000 changes in 1 minute
save ""              # disables RDB entirely
```

Any one save point triggering is enough: whichever fires first starts a save.
More save points mean fresher snapshots under load, at the cost of more fork
and disk work.

### How BGSAVE works: fork plus copy-on-write

`BGSAVE` forks the server process:

- The child writes the snapshot to a temp file and atomically renames it over
  the old RDB; the parent keeps serving clients uninterrupted.
- Fork is cheap because the child shares the parent's memory pages via
  **copy-on-write** — until one of them writes to a page, both read the same
  physical copy. The snapshot therefore captures the dataset as it was at fork
  time.
- The cost concentrates in two places: the **fork itself** stalls the main
  thread (watch `latest_fork_usec` in `INFO persistence` — it grows with memory
  pressure), and under heavy writes the COW copies can **spike memory** while
  the save runs.
- The synchronous `SAVE` command also exists — it blocks everything and is
  effectively only for debugging.

RDB strengths: compact file, fast restarts, exactly one point-in-time artifact
per save. RDB weakness: everything after the last completed snapshot vanishes
on failure — minutes of writes, gone.

## AOF: the append-only log

With `appendonly yes`, every write command is appended to the AOF as it
executes. Recovery replays the log. Durability is a dial called `appendfsync`:

| Policy | Behavior | Crash window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `always` | fsync after every write | worst case: the in-flight command |
| `everysec` (default) | background thread fsyncs once per second | about 1–2 seconds |
| `no` | the OS decides when to flush | unbounded, server-dependent |

`always` is the safest and the slowest — every write waits on disk. `everysec`
is the pragmatic default: a compromise that guarantees at most ~1 second of
loss in exchange for nearly unperturbed write speed. `no` hands durability to
the OS page cache: never lose *more* than the cache holds, but never know
exactly how much either.

If the AOF is truncated by a crash mid-write, `redis-check-aof` can repair the
tail; if a write command arrived while the disk was full, the server is
configured to keep answering reads but reject writes (write commands fail
with a `MISCONF` error until the AOF is repaired) rather than silently
diverge from the log.

## AOF rewrite: compacting the log

Replay time grows with log length, so the AOF is periodically **rewritten**:
`BGREWRITEAOF` forks (same COW mechanics as `BGSAVE`) and walks the *current*
dataset, emitting the minimal set of commands that recreates it — a thousand
`INCR`s against one key become one `SET`. The original keeps receiving writes
while the child works; the new log then replays far faster.

Rewrites trigger automatically when the log outgrows its baseline:

```text
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100   # when AOF is 100% bigger than last rewrite
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb    # ...and at least this big
```

### The hybrid preamble

Since Redis 5, `aof-use-rdb-preamble yes` (the default) makes every rewrite
write a full **RDB snapshot as the preamble** of the AOF, followed by the
incremental commands since the rewrite. You get RDB's fast load speed for the
bulk of the data and AOF's fine-grained durability for the tail — the "hybrid"
persistence the exam expects you to recognize.

## What loads at restart

The load rules are short and absolute:

- **AOF enabled** → Redis loads the AOF and ignores the RDB file. AOF wins
  because it is the more durable record.
- **AOF disabled** → Redis loads `dump.rdb`.
- With hybrid AOF, the load is the RDB preamble plus the AOF tail.

## Risk windows, config by config

- RDB only: lose everything since the last *successful* save — with the
  defaults above, potentially an hour or more on a quiet dataset, and a save
  that failed (full disk) silently extends the window.
- AOF `everysec`: lose roughly the last second — the standard choice.
- AOF `always`: lose at most the command in flight.
- RDB + AOF: the AOF window applies; the RDB is a fast-restart and backup
  artifact, not the durability source.
- No persistence: everything after restart is gone — correct for a cache,
  catastrophic for a system of record.

Replication is a separate durability axis: a replica holds a copy, but async
replication has its own loss window, and a `FLUSHALL` propagates — persistence
and replication complement, never replace, each other.

## Exam takeaways

- RDB = compact point-in-time snapshots via `BGSAVE`: fork + copy-on-write;
  the fork stall (`latest_fork_usec`) and COW memory spike are the costs.
- Save points are "N changes within M seconds" thresholds; `save ""` disables
  RDB; the snapshot covers only the moment of the fork.
- `appendfsync always` / `everysec` / `no` trade durability against write
  latency; `everysec` is the default with a ~1–2 second window.
- `BGREWRITEAOF` compacts the log to the minimal replay of the current state,
  and `aof-use-rdb-preamble` makes the rewrite an RDB body — hybrid persistence.
- At restart, AOF (if enabled) always beats the RDB file.
